paper.title: Advanced Tool Learning and Selection System (ATLASS): A Closed-Loop Framework Using LLM
paper.central_claim: ATLASS: a closed-loop multi-agent LLM framework that analyzes tasks, retrieves or generates (code-writer/executor loop, web-doc grounded for APIs) tools on demand, stores them in a tool database for reuse, and thereby solves tasks with lower inference cost and broader capability than LATM.

provenance.notes: Opus aggregate seat via the configured claude-kimi type fable; no route probing. actual_model/session_id/receipt_ref are null because the subagent runtime exposes no verifiable provider receipt to this worker.

sections_read: Opus: complete pinned text read end-to-end (abstract, all sections, tables, appendices) before opening seat records; targeted re-reads for every disputed field

evidence.support_explanation: Persistent registry links descriptions to Python functions.

evidence.quote: The process operates in a loop, continuously executing until it locates a workable code base.
evidence.support_explanation: Runtime error feedback repairs tool and admits it; no semantic test or finite stopping budget.

evidence.quote: Once it finds a working code base, it adds its information and the tool’s information back to the Tool Dataset.

evidence.support_explanation: Human credential supply needed for API tools.

evidence.support_explanation: Database-present comparison supports limited inference amortization.

evidence.quote: The framework requires human feedback before running any Python code generated by the model

evidence.quote: Tool Selection Accuracy
evidence.support_explanation: Section titled 'accuracy' reports no accuracy number; Table I is a single qualitative example of one tool and three alternative prompts.

evidence.quote: is reusable by the list of Alternative Prompts
evidence.support_explanation: Reuse demonstrated by authors' claim on one example; no execution check that the tool actually solves the alternative prompts.

evidence.quote: LATM can only generate tools that rely solely on Python
evidence.support_explanation: Claim about LATM's limits; Table II is a checkmark matrix over 8 task/tool pairs (ATLASS all checked; LATM unchecked for charting, stock, web search) with no run results, no success criterion and no LATM execution described.

evidence.quote: we have consumed 2895 tokens and an average cost of 0.1008 USD per prompt when the tool is not available
evidence.support_explanation: Table III averages over 8 prompts reproduce (23163/8 and 15364/8): 2895 vs 1920 tokens and 0.1008 vs 0.0624 USD with gpt-4-0613; same prompts appear to be rerun with and without the tool, one run each.

evidence.quote: does a better job of solving complex problems than similar research
evidence.support_explanation: Headline superiority claim is not backed by any task-success or accuracy measurement in the paper.

evidence.quote: Quantitative evaluation of the framework
evidence.support_explanation: Authors list quantitative comparison with other pipelines as future work and note single-model (GPT-4) testing.

evidence.quote: The overall cost is minimized by utilizing smaller model variations, such as GPT-3.5.
evidence.support_explanation: Cost-minimization via GPT-3.5 is asserted, not measured; Limitations also state GPT-3.5/open-source use is future work.

evidence.quote: Apply other models like ChatGPT 3.5 or open-source LLM for less demanding tasks like Task Analyzer and Tool Selector and compare results.
evidence.support_explanation: Contradicts §IV-C's 'overall cost is minimized by utilizing ... GPT-3.5' (son55:E011): the GPT-3.5 saving is future work, all measured runs used gpt-4-0613.

signatures.object: Tool library: JSON metadata + Python tool implementations, grown across queries; baseline = LATM-style per-task tool or no stored tools
signatures.information: User query, tool DB contents, web documentation via SerpAPI for API tools, user-supplied API key inserted by regex (not shown to the model)
signatures.operation: Task Analyzer splits query -> Tool Master lists needed tools -> Tool Selector (LLM matches to DB, semantic equivalence) -> if absent, code-writer/executor loop generates, annotates, runs until it works -> register in DB
signatures.output: New or retrieved callable tools used by Task Solver
signatures.conditions: generate only when no similar tool present; human reviews code before execution
signatures.feedback: Interpreter errors/tracebacks to the code writer
signatures.selection_rule: executes without error; Selector LLM equivalence judgement; no test-based acceptance
signatures.selection_data: the tool-generating prompt itself; no validation set (unlike LATM's validation set as described by the authors)
signatures.later_use: Tool Selector queries the DB for later requirements
signatures.claimed_effect: per-prompt tokens 2895 -> 1920 and USD 0.1008 -> 0.0624 when tool already in DB (8 prompts, gpt-4-0613)
signatures.failure_boundary: Wrong-but-running tools persist; mis-matched tool reuse not measured; API-based and complex tools listed as limitation; single model

signatures.object: Per-query multi-agent pipeline (Task Analyzer, Tool Master, Task Solver)
signatures.operation: static decomposition into subtasks and tool requirements

gap.author_gap: Human-designed tools are inflexible; prior tool makers (LATM) create task-specific tools that are not reusable across similar queries and cannot use external libraries or APIs.
gap.checked_gap: Plausible limitation of per-task tool making, but the statements about LATM are the authors' characterization (no LATM run or text pinned); related-work coverage is broad but mostly off-topic (pre-training, LoRA) and omits other tool/skill-library work.
lineage: LATM (tool maker, validation-set check) -> ConAgents (three agents for selection/execution/calibration) -> ATLASS (analysis + selector + generator + persistent DB + web-grounded API tools)
gap.closest_adjacent: LATM, ConAgents, AutoAgents, AvaTaR as characterized in the Literature Review; no original texts pinned, no comparison run
gap.residue: Reuse of generated tools across paraphrased tasks; external API tools.
gap.stakes: Per-query token/cost saving of about one third when the tool exists (8 prompts).
gap.method_response: Selector matches by semantic description, generator uses web docs for APIs, DB persists tools.
gap.remaining_gap: Correctness validation of generated tools, quantified selector accuracy, benchmark task success, retirement/versioning of tools.

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: RS 'by-products into reusable capital' corresponds to registering generated tools; interpreter feedback corresponds to the H07 repair loop.

assessment.evidence_level_note: Even task-level success is not measured; the only retained-artifact effect is lower token cost when a tool is already stored, apparently on the same 8 prompts.
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: Author-reported, gpt-4-0613, 8 illustrative prompts: a generate-repair-register tool pipeline can produce and reuse tools, and re-running a prompt whose tool is stored costs ~34% fewer tokens (2895→1920). 'Better than similar research' is unsupported; the authors list quantitative comparison as future work.
